title: Filter Structures
description: Realize a transfer function as a network: flow graphs, direct and transposed forms, cascade and parallel sections, FIR structures and the lattice.

study.title: Block diagrams and signal-flow graphs
study.body: A filter program only adds, multiplies by constants and stores past values. A **block diagram** draws exactly that: adders (⊗ circles here), gains and unit delays $z^{-1}$ (boxes marked D). A **signal-flow graph** is the same network in shorthand: each node is a variable equal to the sum of the signals arriving on its branches, and each branch multiplies by its gain or by $z^{-1}$. The network can be computed sample by sample only if every loop contains at least one delay. Different networks with the same $H(z)$ differ in memory, operation count and, as unit 7 shows, in sensitivity to finite word length.

study.title: Direct form II
study.body: O&S write the denominator as $1 - \sum a_kz^{-k}$, so the feedback gains $a_k$ are **added** (watch the sign when comparing with other books). Direct form I realizes the zeros and then the poles with separate delay lines ($M + N$ delays). Swapping the two parts lets them share one delay line holding $w[n], w[n-1], \ldots$: **direct form II**, with $\max(M, N)$ delays (canonic). Both need $M + N + 1$ multipliers and $M + N$ two-input additions.

study.title: Transposed forms
study.body: **Transposition theorem**: reverse every branch, swap input and output, and turn branch points into adders and adders into branch points: the transfer function does not change. Transposed direct form II computes $y[n] = b_0x[n] + s_1[n-1]$ first and updates the states afterwards. It has the same counts as direct form II, but its additions happen in the state variables, which often behaves better in fixed point.
study.formula: \begin{aligned} y[n] &= b_0x[n] + s_1[n-1] \\ s_1[n] &= b_1x[n] + a_1y[n] + s_2[n-1] \\ s_2[n] &= b_2x[n] + a_2y[n] \end{aligned}

study.title: Cascade form
study.body: Factor numerator and denominator and group the roots in **second-order sections** (SOS) with real coefficients: each complex pole pair (and zero pair) stays together; real roots can be paired up. An order-$N$ filter becomes $\lceil N/2\rceil$ sections in series, typically each in direct form II or its transpose: 5 multipliers and 2 delays per section. Each pole pair now depends on only two coefficients, which makes the cascade far more robust than one high-order direct form.

study.title: Parallel form
study.body: A partial-fraction expansion writes $H(z)$ as a constant (or short FIR part, when $M \ge N$) plus second-order sections whose numerators are only first order, $e_{0k} + e_{1k}z^{-1}$. The sections run side by side and their outputs are added. Like the cascade it keeps each pole pair local; the zeros, however, are formed by the sum of all branches and are more sensitive.

study.title: FIR structures
study.body: An FIR filter needs no feedback: a **tapped delay line** (direct form) with $M$ delays, $M + 1$ multipliers and $M$ adders; its transpose is the same with the adders between the delays. Linear-phase filters share each coefficient between two taps: add $x[n-k] + x[n-M+k]$ first, then multiply, which roughly halves the multiplications ($M/2 + 1$ for type I). FIR filters can also be cascaded in sections, e.g. to keep zero quadruples together.

study.title: Explore: the FIR lattice
study.body: A **lattice** builds $A(z) = 1 - \sum \alpha_mz^{-m}$ from $M$ identical stages, each with one coefficient $k_i$ (a reflection coefficient), used twice. Stage $i$: $e_i[n] = e_{i-1}[n] - k_i\tilde{e}_{i-1}[n-1]$ and $\tilde{e}_i[n] = -k_ie_{i-1}[n] + \tilde{e}_{i-1}[n-1]$. For two stages $\alpha_2 = k_2$ and $\alpha_1 = k_1(1 - k_2)$. All zeros lie inside the unit circle exactly when every $|k_i| < 1$: drag $k_2$ past ±1 and watch a zero leave. Lattices are popular in speech coding and adaptive filters.

steps.title: Three building blocks
steps.body: Every LTI filter can be built from adders (circles), constant multipliers and unit delays $z^{-1}$ (boxes marked D). Following O&S, the feedback coefficients are **added**: $H(z) = \frac{\sum b_kz^{-k}}{1 - \sum a_kz^{-k}}$. (The Discrete-Time Signals & Systems subject wrote $1 + \sum a_kz^{-k}$, so there the same filter has feedback coefficients of opposite sign.) In the first-order direct form II below, the state $w[n] = x[n] + a_1w[n-1]$ feeds both the feedback and the output $y[n] = b_0w[n] + b_1w[n-1]$.

steps.prompt: Find the impulse response of this direct form II filter (all adders add, initially at rest).

steps.title: Signal-flow graphs
steps.body: A signal-flow graph strips a block diagram to its essence: **nodes** are signals, **branches** carry a gain or a delay, and each node value is the sum of everything arriving on its branches. To compute the output sample by sample, every loop must contain a delay; otherwise a node would depend on its own current value.
steps.formula: w_j[n] = \sum_{\text{branches } i \to j} (\text{gain or } z^{-1}) \cdot w_i[n]

steps.prompt: A flow graph containing a loop without any delay element cannot be computed one sample at a time with ordinary arithmetic.
steps.explanation: In a delay-free loop a node's current value depends on itself: $w[n] = x[n] + c\,w[n]$. Computing it needs solving an equation (here $w[n] = x[n]/(1 - c)$), not a simple sequence of additions and multiplications. Practical structures always put at least one $z^{-1}$ in every loop.

steps.prompt: This second-order direct form II filter has $H(z) = \frac{b_0 + b_1z^{-1} + b_2z^{-2}}{1 - a_1z^{-1} - a_2z^{-2}}$. Tap every multiplier that affects the **poles**.
steps.explanation: The poles are the roots of $1 - a_1z^{-1} - a_2z^{-2}$: only the feedback gains $a_1$ and $a_2$ enter. The $b_k$ on the right form the zeros. The delays are shared by both parts, which is what makes direct form II canonic.

steps.title: Reading a transfer function off a diagram
steps.body: In direct form II the left column of gains sets the denominator and the right column the numerator. At DC every $z^{-1}$ becomes 1, so the gain is the sum of the feed-forward gains over one minus the sum of the feedback gains.

steps.prompt: Find the DC gain $H(e^{j0})$ of this direct form II filter (all adders add).
steps.explanation: Read the gains off the diagram: $b_0, b_1, b_2$ = {{b0}}, {{b1}}, {{b2}} and $a_1, a_2$ = {{a1}}, {{a2}}, so $H(z) = \frac{b_0 + b_1z^{-1} + b_2z^{-2}}{1 - a_1z^{-1} - a_2z^{-2}}$. At $z = 1$: $\frac{b_0 + b_1 + b_2}{1 - a_1 - a_2}$ = {{b0+b1+b2}} / {{1-a1-a2}} = {{(b0+b1+b2)/(1-a1-a2)||3}}. Mind the signs: the adders add $a_1w[n-1]$ and $a_2w[n-2]$, which puts minus signs in the denominator.

steps.prompt: Match each element of a signal-flow graph to its meaning.
pairs: sum of all incoming branch signals
steps.explanation: A flow graph is a picture of a set of linear equations: each node equation sums its incoming branches, each branch scales or delays. The source node has no incoming branches; the sink node is the output.

steps.title: Transposed direct form II
steps.body: Reverse all branches and swap input and output: the transfer function stays the same. The transposed direct form II computes the output first, $y[n] = b_0x[n] + s_1[n-1]$, then updates its states.
steps.formula: \begin{aligned} s_1[n] &= b_1x[n] + a_1y[n] + s_2[n-1] \\ s_2[n] &= b_2x[n] + a_2y[n] \end{aligned}

steps.prompt: A first-order transposed direct form II filter computes $y[n] = {{b0}}x[n] + s[n-1]$, then $s[n] = {{b1}}x[n] + ({{a1}})y[n]$. The input is a unit step $x[n] = u[n]$, and $s[-1] = 0$.

steps.title: Cascade of second-order sections
steps.body: Factor $H(z)$ and group conjugate pole pairs and zero pairs into second-order sections with real coefficients. An order-$N$ filter becomes $\lceil N/2\rceil$ sections in series, each with up to 5 multipliers and 2 delays.

steps.prompt: An order-{{N}} IIR filter (numerator also of order {{N}}) is built as a cascade of second-order sections in direct form II, 5 multipliers each.

ask.explanation: Each section realizes two poles and two zeros: {{N}} / 2 = {{N/2}} sections.
{{N/2}} sections × 5 ($b_{0k}, b_{1k}, b_{2k}, a_{1k}, a_{2k}$) = {{5*N/2}}. One direct form II would need $2N + 1$ = {{2*N+1}}: the cascade costs a few more multipliers but is much more robust.
2 delays per section × {{N/2}} sections = {{N}}: as few as one canonic direct form II.

steps.prompt: Two first-order sections $\frac{1}{1 - {{p1}}z^{-1}}$ and $\frac{1}{1 - ({{p2}})z^{-1}}$ are cascaded. Find $h[2]$ of the cascade.
steps.explanation: The impulse responses are $p_1^n$ and $p_2^n$; the cascade convolves them: $h[2] = \sum_{k=0}^{2} p_1^kp_2^{2-k} = p_2^2 + p_1p_2 + p_1^2$ = {{p2^2}} + ({{p1*p2}}) + {{p1^2}} = {{p1^2 + p1*p2 + p2^2}}.

steps.title: Parallel form
steps.body: A partial-fraction expansion turns $H(z)$ into a sum of low-order sections (plus a constant when the numerator order is not lower than the denominator order). The sections run side by side on the same input, and their outputs are added.

steps.prompt: Match each structure to its defining property.
steps.explanation: All four realize the same $H(z)$ in exact arithmetic. They differ in how the coefficients relate to the poles and zeros and in the order of the operations, which matters once coefficients and signals are rounded (next unit).

steps.prompt: An order-{{N}} IIR filter has a numerator of order {{N}} too.

ask.prompt: How many delays does direct form I need?
ask.explanation: Separate delay lines for the inputs ({{N}}) and the outputs ({{N}}): {{2*N}}.

ask.prompt: How many delays does direct form II need?
How many two-input additions does direct form II need per output sample?
ask.explanation: The feedback adder combines $x[n]$ with {{N}} products: {{N}} additions. The output adds {{N+1}} products: another {{N}}. In total $M + N$ = {{2*N}} two-input additions per sample.

steps.prompt: A linear-phase FIR filter has {{L}} taps (order $M$ = {{L-1}}).

ask.prompt: How many multipliers does the plain direct form use?
How many multipliers does the folded (symmetric) structure use?
ask.explanation: Taps $k$ and $M - k$ share a coefficient: add the two delayed samples, then multiply. {{L}} taps give $\lceil {{L}}/2 \rceil$ = {{ceil(L/2)}} multipliers (the centre tap of an odd length has no partner).
An FIR filter of order $M$ stores $M$ past inputs: {{L-1}} delays, in both forms.

steps.prompt: A two-stage FIR lattice has reflection coefficients $k_1$ = {{k1}} and $k_2$ = {{k2}}. It realizes $A(z) = 1 - \alpha_1z^{-1} - \alpha_2z^{-2}$.

ask.explanation: The last stage sets the highest coefficient directly: $\alpha_2 = k_2$ = {{k2}}.

steps.prompt: The zeros of a two-stage lattice $A(z)$ are shown with $k_1$ = {{k1}}. Set $k_2$ so that the zeros form a complex pair of radius {{r}} (dashed circle).
steps.explanation: $A(z) = 1 - \alpha_1z^{-1} - \alpha_2z^{-2}$ has zeros with product $-\alpha_2 = -k_2$. For a complex pair that product is $r^2$, so $k_2 = -r^2$ = {{-r^2}}. With $|k_2| < 1$ the zeros stay inside the unit circle, as the lattice theorem promises.

steps.prompt: Convert $A(z) = 1 - ({{a1}})z^{-1} - ({{a2}})z^{-2}$ into a two-stage lattice. Find $k_1$.
Transposing a filter structure changes its transfer function into the time-reversed one.
steps.explanation: The transposition theorem says that reversing all branches and swapping input and output leaves $H(z)$ **unchanged** (for single-input single-output networks). Only the internal order of operations changes, which can matter for round-off and overflow.

steps.prompt: $H(z) = \frac{1 + 2z^{-1} + z^{-2}}{1 - 0.5z^{-1} + 0.25z^{-2}}$. Which structure realizes it with only two delays?
options: Two first-order sections in parallel, each in direct form I
None: it always needs four delays
steps.explanation: Direct form II shares one delay line between numerator and denominator: $\max(2, 2) = 2$ delays. Direct form I needs $2 + 2 = 4$. The poles here are complex ($0.25 \pm 0.43j$), so a real parallel split into first-order sections is impossible anyway.

steps.prompt: A second-order section has the denominator $1 - a_1z^{-1} - a_2z^{-2}$ with $a_1$ = {{c1||4}} and $a_2$ = {{c2||4}} (complex poles).

ask.prompt: Find the pole angle $\theta$ in rad.

steps.prompt: An application can use an order-{{N}} elliptic IIR filter (cascade of second-order sections, 5 multipliers each) or a linear-phase FIR filter of order {{M}} (folded structure), both at $f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: How many multiplications per second does the IIR filter need?
How many times as many does the FIR filter need?
ask.explanation: FIR: $M/2 + 1$ = {{M/2+1}} per sample against {{5*N/2}} for the IIR: {{(M/2+1)/(5*N/2)||3}} times as many. The price of exactly linear phase.

steps.prompt: A direct form II section computes $w[n] = x[n] + {{a1}}w[n-1] + ({{a2}})w[n-2]$ and $y[n] = {{b0}}w[n] + ({{b1}})w[n-1] + {{b2}}w[n-2]$. Find $h[2]$.
A polynomial $A(z) = 1 - \sum_{m=1}^{M}\alpha_mz^{-m}$ has all its zeros strictly inside the unit circle exactly when all reflection coefficients of its lattice satisfy $|k_i| < 1$.
steps.explanation: This is the key property of the lattice (it underlies the Schur–Cohn stability test). It also means that the all-pole lattice $1/A(z)$ is stable if and only if every $|k_i| < 1$: stability can be checked, or guaranteed under quantization, coefficient by coefficient.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of turning a high-order $H(z)$ into a cascade of second-order sections in order.
items: Find the poles and zeros (roots of denominator and numerator)
Pair each complex pole pair with the zero pair closest to it
Form second-order sections with real coefficients from each pair
Order the sections and scale them to prevent overflow
steps.explanation: The roots come first. Pairing poles with nearby zeros keeps each section's gain modest (a zero partly cancels the peak of its pole pair). Conjugate pairs give real coefficients. Finally the section order and scale factors are chosen for overflow and round-off noise, the subject of the next unit.
